title: Signature-based isolation and smart throttling — PRD draft
content:
Purpose
This document proposes a new approach to dedicated pool isolation and overload handling: signature-based isolation combined with a smart throttling fabric. The goal is to reduce SLO violations during transient surges while preserving economic efficiency and minimizing manual tuning for tenants.

Context / Motivation
Current approaches we have explored rely heavily on static quotas, burst credit pools, or coarse priority lanes. Those tools work but either (a) require ops intervention to tune fairness, (b) lead to blunt preemptions that cause sudden quality regressions, or (c) allow noisy flows (short, chatty evals; large offline batch jobs) to consume disproportionate headroom during microbursts.

We need a way to:
- Recognize classes of traffic by runtime signature rather than only by tenant-ID or queue weight.
- Temporarily and predictably shape noisy flows while allowing interactive, latency-sensitive requests to keep SLOs.
- Make preemption/throttling decisions explainable and simulatable so product and SRE can reason about customer impact.

High-level idea
1) Traffic signatures: compute a compact signature per request stream describing key dimensions: request token length distribution, model family, async vs sync, concurrency patterns, KV-cache reuse ratio (inferred), and error/retry behavior. Signatures are hashed and clustered on the control plane to form soft traffic classes.
2) Soft lanes and weighted token buckets: for each soft class we attach a tunable token-bucket that describes burst allowance and steady-state throughput. Buckets are elastically provisioned against a pool of headroom credits that the pool manager can reassign in real time.
3) Smart throttling fabric: a request scoring function uses signature, tenant priority, current bucket state, and downstream latency headroom to decide: allow immediately, enqueue to low-latency backlog, slow-path (reduced batch size / small-quantization), or politely reject with suggested retry windows. Decisions are recorded for auditing and simulated in the capacity simulator.

Goals & success metrics
- SLO preservation: 95th percentile latency for interactive requests should remain within target during 99% of historical microburst events simulated.
- Fairness: no tenant should consume >X% of transient headroom for more than 5 consecutive minutes in the simulator scenarios (configurable).
- Explainability: for any throttled request we can surface the top-3 reasons (signature rule, bucket exhaustion, higher-priority preemption) in console traces.
- Low ops overhead: policies should adapt without manual per-tenant tuning for at least 80% of customers.

Detailed behavior
- Signature extraction: lightweight, per-connection rolling counters produced at the ingress layer. Signatures are ephemeral (TTL minutes) and only summarized as hashed keys to the control plane (no PII).
- Class formation: control plane periodically clusters signatures using streaming k-means (small k) and emits class IDs to the runtime. Clusters are constrained by policy (e.g., deduce interactive vs batch).
- Bucket semantics: buckets have (capacity, refill-rate, decay-policy). Capacity is backed by a shared headroom ledger; when headroom is low, buckets decay faster for noisy classes.
- Decision flow: request -> signature lookup -> token check -> scoring -> route/policy. Scoring uses simple arithmetic and thresholds so decisions stay deterministic and observable.

Preemption and degradation modes (graceful ladder)
1) Non-destructive soft-throttle: slow-path that keeps request accepted but limits concurrency or enforces smaller micro-batches. Suitable for background re-ranking or embeddings jobs.
2) Deferred execution: low-priority requests are delayed/queued with user-visible ETA and optional webhook callback when executed.
3) Quality-reduced path: runtime automatically selects a faster quantized model variant with lower cost for non-interactive classes.
4) Preemptive reject: final step when capacity is exhausted and tenant is exceeding allowed transient share; reply includes retry-after and suggested backoff.

Simulator & safety checks
We will extend the capacity simulator to:
- Replay historical traffic with signature reconstruction.
- Run adversarial scenarios (many tenants shift from low cost batch to chatty interactive suddenly).
- Output per-tenant impact: latency, error rates, % headroom consumed.
- Validate rollback criteria (if SLO regressions > threshold when policy is live, auto-scale fallback triggers).

Operational UX
- Console: show aggregated signatures (human-readable labels), per-class token-bucket state, and live suggested mitigations.
- Alerts: automated detection of signature drift (new heavy chatty pattern) and suggested policy recipes.
- Audit logs: for each throttle decision include class ID, reason codes, and affected request IDs for debugging.

Implementation plan (phases)
Phase 0 (spike, 3w): build signature proto, simple clusterer, runtime signature emitter, and a local simulator toy.
Phase 1 (iter 1, 6w): integrate token-bucket fabric, scoring code path, and console UI for live metrics. Canary on small set of dedicated pools.
Phase 2 (scale, 8w): rollout clustering to control plane, add decay policies, and integrate quality-reduced model routing.
Phase 3 (safety & polish, 4w): add auditability, rollback hooks, and hard policy gates for regulated tenants.

Risks & mitigations
- Incorrect signature mapping could misclassify tenant traffic: mitigate with canary and manual override per-tenant.
- Complexity of cluster tuning: keep clustering conservative (small k) and expose easy toggles in console.
- Privacy concerns: signatures must be aggregated and hashed; no user prompt content leaves the runtime in cleartext beyond existing logging.

Open questions / decisions to make
- How long do we persist class assignments? (minutes vs hours)
- Default headroom sharing policy between enterprise tiers and self-serve customers?
- Acceptable fairness window sizes and telemetry thresholds.

Immediate next steps
- Align with SRE on simulator inputs and rollback thresholds.
- Engineering spike to validate cheap signature extraction at ingress.
- Product review with CS to surface likely customer-visible behaviors and documentation needs.

Notes to reviewers
This is intentionally a mid-fidelity draft focusing on the runtime control loop and operational consequences. Looking for feedback on: (1) whether classing by runtime signature is actionable for our pools, (2) appropriate fairness windows, and (3) console UX minimums for explainability.
summary: Draft PRD for signature-based traffic classification and smart throttling for dedicated capacity. Proposes soft lanes via token-buckets, a scoring-based decision flow, simulator integration, graceful degradation modes, and an implementation roadmap.
